title: Effects of ischemic, low-load, and BFR-based preconditioning strategies to attenuate BFR exercise-induced muscle damage
summary:
Blood flow restriction training (BFR training) is a training method in which cuffs are used to partially restrict blood flow to the muscles. This allows similar training effects to be achieved with very low weights as with classic strength training with high loads. This method is particularly interesting for rehabilitation, as it puts less strain on the joints.

However, little research has been done to date on whether BFR training causes muscle damage, which manifests itself, for example, as muscle soreness or temporary loss of strength. The aim of this study is to investigate whether certain forms of “preloading” (preconditioning) can protect the muscles from such damage. To this end, we are comparing different methods: a classic warm-up, training with cuff pressure, pure blood flow restriction without movement, and no preconditioning.

The results should help to make BFR training safer and enable recommendations for practical use to be derived, particularly in rehabilitation and prevention programs.

interventions.name:
At the beginning, the test subjects undergo an anamnesis, in which possible exclusion criteria are checked on the basis of a questionnaire on existing diseases. This is followed by randomised and equal allocation to the four groups (C1 to C4). 

All participants first undergo an identical initial
• Group C2 completes a traditional warm-up consisting of three sets of 15 repetitions at 30% of 1RM without cuff pressure (0% AOP), with a five-minute break between sets.

• Group C3 performs the same training protocol, but under low-pressure BFR conditions at 50% AOP. After completing the last repetition of each set, cuff pressure is maintained until a total occlusion time of five minutes is reached. This is followed by a five-minute reperfusion phase before the next
• Group C4 receives passive ischemic preconditioning (IPC) in the form of three five-minute occlusion phases at 100% AOP, each followed by five minutes of reperfusion.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Physically active (at least 2 training sessions per week)
Exclusion criteria:
● Injuries or acute or chronic illnesses
● Use of medication or dietary supplements
● Individuals with pre-existing damage to the venous system (e.g., varicose veins, vascular surgery, extremities with dialysis access)
● High blood pressure
● Circulatory and coagulation disorders (e.g., condition after transient ischemic attack, stroke, angina pectoris, heart attack, peripheral arterial disease)
